justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 97.1 is anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing price or index level at the time of the forecast, with only minimal expected movement given typical intraday mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any immediate scheduled catalysts. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 97.5 reflects a marginal positive drift assumption, consistent with historical tendencies for the underlying asset or index to trend mildly upward over short windows when no strong directional signal is present. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises further to 98.5, incorporating a longer-run drift component while still remaining relatively close to the starting level, suggesting I was not anticipating any major directional break in either direction.

The confidence interval widths grow meaningfully as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.2 points, consistent with observed short-term volatility for a moderately volatile asset. By one week, that span widens to 11 points, and by one month it reaches 21 points, roughly consistent with annualized volatility in the 15–20% range depending on the underlying. These widths were shaped primarily by historical realized volatility, the lack of strong near-term anchoring events, and the inherent difficulty of forecasting over longer horizons where macro conditions, sentiment shifts, and liquidity dynamics can diverge substantially from baseline assumptions.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected adverse macro announcement — such as a sharper-than-anticipated central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant data miss on employment or inflation — could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst, a surprise dovish pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bounds. The one-month interval is most vulnerable to being breached simply because a sustained directional trend, once established, can carry prices far beyond what short-term volatility estimates would suggest. Tail events, by definition, are not fully captured in intervals calibrated to historical norms.
